analogy.p: Imagine a **chef** (the CPU) following a **recipe book** (the program) kept on a shelf in the kitchen (RAM). The chef reads one line of the recipe at a time (**fetch**), works out what it means (**decode**) and then does it, such as chopping or mixing (**execute**), before moving on to the next line. The ingredients (data) are on the same shelves as the recipe, just like instructions and data share memory in the Von Neumann design. The analogy breaks down because a chef understands English, whereas the CPU can only follow instructions written in binary machine code, and it works billions of times faster than any person.
analogy.t: A chef working through a recipe

bullets: **Purpose of the CPU**: to process data and instructions by performing the fetch-decode-execute cycle over and over.
Know that the CPU is the part of the computer that **runs programs**: it takes each instruction in turn and carries it out.
Know the **Von Neumann architecture**: one main memory holds both the instructions and the data, and the CPU fetches from it.
Know that the CPU is a **microprocessor**: a single integrated circuit (chip) containing millions or billions of tiny switches called transistors.
Be able to link the CPU to **input, output, main memory (RAM) and secondary storage**.
Later points in 1.1 build on this: the cycle itself, the components (ALU, CU, cache, registers) and performance (clock speed, cache size, cores).
Command words you will meet: **State**, **Identify**, **Describe**, **Explain**, **Give a reason**.
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: OCR J277 section 1.1 (Systems architecture) begins with the **purpose of the CPU**. You must be able to state that the central processing unit (CPU) exists to **process data and instructions** by repeatedly carrying out the **fetch-decode-execute cycle**, and you must understand this inside the **Von Neumann architecture**, where program instructions and data are held together in main memory. This matters because every other part of Paper 1 (components, performance, memory, storage, software) is explained in terms of what the CPU does and what it needs from the rest of the computer. Questions on it are usually short 1 to 3 mark 'state' or 'describe' items, but the idea underpins longer 6 mark answers on performance.

bullets: A CPU is an **integrated circuit** (a whole circuit etched onto a single piece of silicon).
It contains **transistors** acting as switches; modern CPUs have billions of them.
It is fitted to the **motherboard** and needs cooling (heat sink, fan or liquid cooling) because switching generates heat.
Phones, tablets and laptops use a CPU too; in a phone it is often part of a bigger chip called a system on a chip.
The CPU only understands **machine code**: instructions written in **binary** (1s and 0s).
The CPU is **not** the same as the computer, the memory or the hard drive; students lose marks by mixing these up.
'Processor' and 'CPU' are used interchangeably in GCSE answers.
core.p: The CPU is a small, square **microprocessor chip** that sits in a socket on the **motherboard**, usually under a heat sink and fan because it gets hot when working hard. Inside the chip are billions of microscopic **transistors**, which are electronic switches that are either on (1) or off (0). By combining these switches into circuits called logic gates, the CPU can add numbers, compare values and move data. It is often called the **'brain' of the computer**, but a more accurate picture is that it is the part that does the actual calculating and decision making while everything else supplies it with instructions and data or takes away its results.

bullets: **Fetch** the next instruction from main memory (RAM), **decode** it so the CPU knows what to do, then **execute** (carry out) it.
'Process' covers **arithmetic** (add, subtract), **logic/comparison** (is A bigger than B?), and **moving data** between memory and the CPU.
The CPU also **controls** the flow of the program, deciding which instruction comes next, including jumps and loops.
It does not store programs permanently; it **borrows** them from RAM while they run.
**Data** is what the program works on (numbers, text, pixel values); **instructions** are what to do to that data. Both are binary.
A mark-scheme style answer: 'It fetches instructions from memory, decodes them and executes them (repeatedly).'
If the cycle stops (for example a crash or power cut), no further instructions are processed and the computer appears frozen.
core.h: The purpose: process data and instructions
core.p: The official purpose of the CPU is to **process data and instructions**. A **program** is a list of instructions, and the CPU takes them one at a time, works out what each one means and carries it out. Every action a computer appears to perform, from showing a web page to running a game, is broken down into a very large number of tiny instructions such as 'add these two numbers', 'compare these values' or 'copy this value to that location'. The CPU does this by repeating the **fetch-decode-execute cycle** (also called the fetch-execute cycle) continuously for as long as the computer is switched on. A typical CPU repeats this cycle billions of times each second.

bullets: **Machine code** = binary instructions the CPU can run directly, with no translation needed.
High-level code (Python, etc.) and assembly language must be **translated** into machine code before the CPU can use them.
An instruction is often thought of as an **operation** (such as ADD, LOAD, STORE) plus the **data or address** it works on.
Typical simple operations: load a value, store a value, add, subtract, compare, jump to another instruction, stop.
Even one line of high-level code (for example `total = a + b`) turns into **several** machine code instructions.
The **instruction set** is built into the CPU design; different CPU families (for example in PCs and in phones) have different instruction sets.
Speed of a CPU is judged by how many of these tiny instructions it can complete each second.
core.p: A **program** is a set of instructions that tells the computer how to complete a task. When programmers write code in a high-level language such as Python, a **translator** (compiler or interpreter) converts it into **machine code**, the only language the CPU can directly follow. Each machine code instruction is a binary pattern that usually contains two parts: **what to do** and **what to do it to**. The set of all instructions a particular CPU can follow is called its **instruction set**. This is why a program written for one type of CPU may not run on another without being translated again.

bullets: **Stored program concept**: instructions and data are held in the **same memory** as binary values.
The CPU has a **control unit (CU)** to manage the cycle, an **arithmetic logic unit (ALU)** to calculate and compare, **registers** and **cache** for fast temporary storage.
The CPU connects to main memory using **buses** (address, data and control), covered in the next section.
The CPU fetches instructions **sequentially** (one after another) unless an instruction changes the order (a jump or branch).
Special registers in the architecture include the **Program Counter (PC)**, **Memory Address Register (MAR)**, **Memory Data Register (MDR)** and **Accumulator (ACC)**.
Because instructions and data share one memory, a program must be **loaded into RAM** before the CPU can run it.
Advantage: flexible, one design runs any program. A well-known limitation is that instructions and data share the same route to memory, which can slow things down (not needed for GCSE).
core.p: The **Von Neumann architecture** is the design on which almost all modern general-purpose computers are based. Its key idea is the **stored program concept**: both the program **instructions** and the **data** they use are stored together in the same main memory (RAM), in binary, and the CPU fetches them from there one at a time. Because everything sits in one memory, a computer can load any program, run it, then load a different program, without being rebuilt. This is why the same hardware can be a word processor one minute and a game the next.

bullets: Programs and the data they use are **loaded from secondary storage into RAM** when opened.
**RAM is volatile** (contents lost when power off); **secondary storage is non-volatile** (kept without power).
RAM is **faster** than secondary storage but **smaller** and more expensive per gigabyte.
The CPU fetches from **RAM** (or cache, which holds copies of frequently used items), never directly from the hard drive during normal running.
If there is not enough RAM, the computer slows down because the CPU must wait for slower storage (link to performance and virtual memory).
Exam reason: 'Because RAM is much faster to access than secondary storage, so the CPU is not kept waiting.'
core.h: Why instructions must be in RAM
core.p: The CPU can only work directly with information held in **registers**, **cache** and **main memory (RAM)**. Secondary storage such as a hard disk drive (HDD) or solid-state drive (SSD) is far too slow to feed a CPU that runs billions of cycles per second, and it is not connected to the CPU in the way RAM is. So when you open an application, the operating system copies the program from secondary storage into RAM, and then the CPU fetches the instructions from RAM. RAM is much faster than secondary storage but is **volatile**, meaning it loses its contents when the power is turned off.

bullets: **Address bus**: carries the **memory address**; it is **one-way**, from CPU to memory.
**Data bus**: carries **data and instructions**; it is **two-way** (memory to CPU on a read, CPU to memory on a write).
**Control bus**: carries **control signals** (read, write, clock/timing) between the CPU and other components.
A bus is a set of wires: each wire carries one **bit**, so a wider bus carries more bits at once.
Memory address in the MAR is placed on the **address bus**; the item found is returned on the **data bus** into the MDR.
Buses are shared by instructions and data in the Von Neumann design, which is why only one transfer can use them at a time.
core.h: Buses: how the CPU talks to memory
core.p: The CPU and main memory are linked by sets of parallel wires called **buses**, which carry binary signals. There are three: the **address bus** carries the address (location) in memory that the CPU wants to read from or write to; the **data bus** carries the actual data or instruction being transferred; and the **control bus** carries control signals such as 'read' or 'write' and timing signals. You do not need to know bus widths for GCSE, but you should know what each carries and the direction. Without buses the CPU and memory could not exchange the instructions and data that the cycle relies on.

bullets: **Arithmetic**: addition, subtraction, multiplication and division of binary numbers (done by the ALU).
**Logic**: AND, OR, NOT operations on binary values (done by the ALU).
**Comparison**: for example checking whether two numbers are equal or which is larger, so a program can make decisions.
**Data movement**: load from memory to a register; store from a register back to memory.
**Control flow**: jump/branch instructions change the Program Counter so the next instruction is not simply the next address.
**Input/output control**: the CPU coordinates with input and output devices (via the control unit and the operating system).
Seeing a graphic or hearing music is the result of the CPU (and other processors) handling huge numbers of these simple operations per second.
core.h: Types of work the CPU performs
core.p: Although programs look very varied, the CPU only ever performs a small family of basic operations. It can **do arithmetic** (add, subtract and so on) and **logical operations** such as AND, OR and NOT in the **ALU**, **compare** two values, **move data** between memory and registers, and **change which instruction runs next**, which is how selection (if statements) and iteration (loops) are carried out. Everything complicated is built by stringing millions of these simple operations together very quickly. Each is carried out as part of the fetch-decode-execute cycle.

bullets: **Input** devices send data into the computer; the data is placed in memory for the CPU to use.
The **CPU processes** the data by running the program's instructions.
**Output** devices present the result to the user (screen, speaker, printer).
**Main memory (RAM)** holds the running program and its data; **secondary storage** keeps files long term.
The **operating system** manages how programs share the CPU and memory, which links to systems software in section 1.5 of the spec.
A system works only when all parts work together: a very fast CPU with too little RAM will still be slow.
core.h: The CPU in the input-process-output-storage model
core.p: A computer system takes **input**, **processes** it and produces **output**, with **storage** used to keep programs and data. The CPU is the **processing** stage: it receives data from input devices (such as the keyboard or mouse) via memory, processes it by following the program, and sends results to output devices (such as the screen or speakers). It cannot do anything useful on its own, because without memory to supply instructions and data and input and output to connect to people, it has nothing to work on and nowhere to send results. This 'big picture' is often tested by asking you to place the CPU in a system diagram or describe how it works with other components.

bullets: Embedded system = a **computer built into a larger device** to do **one dedicated task** (it is not a general-purpose computer).
Examples: washing machine, microwave oven, central heating controller, smart TV remote, traffic lights, car engine control unit, fitness tracker.
They still contain a **processor, memory and input/output** (sensors and actuators), just in a small, often low-power form.
Because they only do one job, they can be **cheaper, smaller, lower power and more reliable** than a general-purpose computer.
Their program is normally fixed and stored in **ROM or flash memory** so it is not lost when switched off.
A general-purpose computer (PC, laptop) can run many different programs; an embedded system is designed to do just one.
core.p: The OCR specification also lists **embedded systems** in this section. An embedded system is a **computer system with a dedicated function inside a larger device**, for example the controller in a washing machine, a microwave, a car's engine management system or a digital watch. These contain a small CPU (a microcontroller) running a fixed program, usually stored in non-volatile memory, to perform one specific job. A general-purpose computer such as a laptop is different: it has a CPU that can run many different programs chosen by the user.

bullets: 1 hertz = 1 cycle per second; 1 kHz = 1 000 Hz; 1 MHz = 1 000 000 Hz; **1 GHz = 1 000 000 000 Hz** (one billion).
Clock speed in GHz × 1 000 000 000 = **cycles per second**.
A fetch-decode-execute cycle for one instruction may take **more than one clock cycle**, so instructions per second can be fewer than cycles per second.
Higher clock speed = **more instructions per second** = faster, but also more heat and power use.
Increasing clock speed too far makes the CPU overheat, which is why designers also add cores and cache.
Clock speed is compared only between similar CPUs; a CPU with fewer GHz but more cores or cache can be faster for some tasks.
core.h: Clock speed and the heartbeat of the CPU
core.p: The CPU has an internal **clock** that produces regular pulses; each pulse keeps the parts of the CPU in step so that actions happen in the right order. **Clock speed** is the number of clock cycles per second, measured in **hertz (Hz)**. A modern CPU might run at 3.2 GHz, which is 3.2 billion cycles each second. A higher clock speed generally means more instructions can be processed each second, so the computer is faster, although other factors (cache size and number of cores) also matter. Clock speed is not the whole story, but it is the headline figure for CPU performance.

bullets: **Clock speed**: more cycles each second = more instructions processed per second.
**Cache size**: more fast memory next to the CPU = fewer slow trips to RAM = less waiting.
**Number of cores**: each core can run its own fetch-decode-execute cycle, so several instructions or programs can be processed **in parallel**.
A dual-core CPU is not automatically twice as fast: the software must be able to share the work and some tasks cannot be split.
Always link your answer to the purpose: 'so more instructions are fetched, decoded and executed per second'.
Performance questions often ask you to compare two CPUs and **recommend** one, using all three factors.
core.h: Link to performance: clock speed, cache and cores
core.p: The next points in the specification cover the three factors that affect CPU performance. A higher **clock speed** means more cycles per second. More **cache** means more frequently used instructions and data are stored close to the CPU, so it waits less for the slower RAM. More **cores** means the CPU can carry out more than one fetch-decode-execute cycle at the same time, one in each core, which helps when programs are written to share work. Understanding the purpose of the CPU lets you explain why each of these makes the computer quicker: they all increase the number of instructions that can be processed in a given time.

bullets: **Binary**: all instructions and data are stored and processed in binary; characters, images and sound are all binary.
**Translators**: compilers and interpreters convert high-level code to machine code the CPU runs.
**Operating system**: manages memory and decides which process the CPU works on at any moment (multitasking).
**Memory and storage**: RAM, cache, registers and secondary storage form a hierarchy of speed and size.
**Logic gates** (AND, OR, NOT): the ALU is built from these.
**Networks and security**: the CPU performs the processing in servers, routers and your own devices alike.
**Ethical/environmental**: faster CPUs use more power and generate more heat; devices are replaced quickly.
core.p: The purpose of the CPU connects to many other parts of the course, and examiners reward answers that make these links. Binary (data representation in section 1.2) explains why instructions and data are 1s and 0s; the operating system controls which program the CPU works on; and translators explain how human-readable code reaches the CPU as machine code. Logic gates (Boolean logic, section 2.4) are the building blocks of the circuits in the CPU. Thinking of the CPU as the processing hub for all this makes the whole specification feel connected.

bullets: 1 mark: **'Processes data and instructions'** or **'carries out the fetch-decode-execute cycle'**.
2 marks: say it **fetches instructions from memory, decodes them and executes them**, and that this is **repeated**.
Avoid vague words like 'does everything', 'runs the computer' or 'stores files' (storage is not the CPU's job).
Use the keywords: **instruction, data, process, fetch, decode, execute, memory, register, binary**.
For 'why' questions finish with the consequence (for example 'so the CPU does not have to wait').
For 6-mark questions plan: purpose, then each component/factor, then a justified conclusion.
core.h: Writing top-mark answers about the CPU
core.p: Most marks on this topic come from using precise vocabulary and giving a complete statement rather than a vague one. 'The brain of the computer' on its own earns nothing; 'it processes data and instructions by fetching, decoding and executing them' earns the mark. For a two-mark question, give the purpose plus one extra detail (for example, that it does this repeatedly, or that the instructions come from RAM). For longer questions, link to performance: say what changes and the effect on the number of instructions processed per second.

exam: **State / Identify (1 mark)**: one precise fact, such as 'to process data and instructions' or 'fetch-decode-execute'. Do not add extras.
**Describe the purpose of the CPU (2 marks)**: 'It fetches instructions from memory, decodes them and executes them' plus 'repeatedly / billions of times per second'.
**Explain (2 to 3 marks)**: give the point and the reason, using 'so', 'because' or 'which means'. Example: RAM is faster than secondary storage, so the CPU is not kept waiting.
**Von Neumann (1 to 2 marks)**: 'instructions and data are stored together in the same memory' is the model phrase.
**Embedded system (2 marks)**: 'a computer system with a dedicated function' and 'inside a larger device', plus an example such as a washing machine.
**Performance questions (up to 6 marks)**: link each factor to its effect: more cycles per second; less waiting for RAM; several instructions at once. End with a judgement.
**Calculations**: convert GHz to Hz by multiplying by 1 000 000 000 and show each line of working; units are required.
Do not just write 'brain of the computer'; examiners want what it does.
Use the OCR keywords: **instruction, data, fetch, decode, execute, memory, binary**.
Check the number of marks: a 1-mark question wants one fact; a 3-mark question wants three separate points.

mistakes.r: The CPU processes data and instructions. Files are stored in secondary storage; running programs are held in RAM.
mistakes.w: The CPU is the brain and stores all the files.

mistakes.r: The CPU is one component. Memory (RAM), storage, input and output are separate components that work with it.
mistakes.w: The CPU is the same thing as the computer or the memory.

mistakes.r: Programs must first be loaded into RAM; the CPU fetches instructions from RAM (and cache), which is much faster than the hard drive.
mistakes.w: The CPU runs the programs directly from the hard drive.

mistakes.r: Its purpose is to process data and instructions by performing the fetch-decode-execute cycle. Speed depends on clock speed, cache and cores.
mistakes.w: The purpose of the CPU is to make the computer fast.

mistakes.r: Von Neumann architecture means instructions and data are stored together in the same main memory (stored program concept).
mistakes.w: Von Neumann means the computer has a CPU.

mistakes.r: RAM is volatile: it loses its contents when power is lost. Secondary storage is non-volatile.
Higher clock speed helps, but cache size and number of cores also affect performance; the answer must refer to instructions processed per second.
mistakes.w: A higher GHz always means a better CPU.

mistakes.r: Each core can run its own cycle so it can be faster, but only if the software can share the work; it is not automatically double.
mistakes.w: A dual-core CPU is exactly twice as fast.

mistakes.r: An embedded system is a computer with a dedicated function inside a larger device, such as a microwave or washing machine.
mistakes.w: An embedded system is a small laptop.

summary: OCR J277 1.1 asks you to state that the purpose of the CPU is to process data and instructions by repeatedly performing the fetch-decode-execute cycle, within the Von Neumann architecture where instructions and data share main memory. It matters because every other idea in systems architecture (components, performance, memory, embedded systems) is explained in terms of what the CPU does.

terms.d: The component that processes data and instructions by carrying out the fetch-decode-execute cycle.
A CPU built as a single integrated circuit (chip) containing millions or billions of transistors.
A single command in machine code that tells the CPU to perform one basic operation.
A set of instructions that tells a computer how to complete a task.
The values (numbers, text, images, sound) that a program uses and processes, stored in binary.
Instructions in binary that the CPU can execute directly without translation.
The repeated process in which the CPU fetches an instruction from memory, decodes it and executes it.
A computer design in which program instructions and data are stored together in the same main memory and fetched by the CPU.
The idea that instructions are held in memory as binary, in the same way as data, so that the CPU can fetch them.
Volatile memory that holds the programs and data currently in use so the CPU can access them quickly.
Memory that loses its contents when the power is turned off.
A set of parallel wires that carries signals between components; the main buses are the address bus, data bus and control bus.
The number of clock cycles the CPU performs each second, measured in hertz (Hz).
A computer system with a dedicated function that is built into a larger device.
A tiny electronic switch used to build the circuits in a CPU; it is either on (1) or off (0).
The complete set of machine code instructions that a particular CPU can understand and execute.

worked.ans: The CPU processes data and instructions. It does this by repeatedly fetching each instruction from memory, decoding it and then executing it (the fetch-decode-execute cycle).
worked.q: Describe the purpose of the CPU. [2 marks]
steps: Mark 1: say what it processes: data and instructions.
Mark 2: say how: by fetching, decoding and executing instructions, and that this is repeated (the fetch-decode-execute cycle).

worked.ans: The CPU fetches instructions from RAM. RAM is much faster to access than the solid-state drive, so copying the game into RAM means the CPU is not kept waiting for instructions and data, and the game runs smoothly.
worked.q: A user opens a game stored on the computer's solid-state drive. Explain why the game is copied into RAM before it runs. [3 marks]
steps: The CPU can only fetch instructions from RAM, cache or its registers, not directly from storage in normal operation (point 1).
RAM is much faster to access than secondary storage (point 2).
So the CPU does not have to wait for instructions or data, which keeps the game running smoothly (consequence, point 3).

worked.q: A CPU has a clock speed of 3.2 GHz and on average each instruction takes 4 clock cycles. Calculate how many instructions it can process in one second. [3 marks]
steps: Convert GHz to Hz: 3.2 GHz = 3.2 × 1 000 000 000 = 3 200 000 000 cycles per second.
Divide by the cycles needed for each instruction: 3 200 000 000 ÷ 4.
